cases.abstract: Personalizing a text-to-image diffusion model requires preserving a specific subject while allowing prompts to change its context and appearance. We introduce DreamBooth, which fine-tunes pretrained models on three to five subject images, associating a rare-token identifier with the subject and its class. The class descriptor connects the instance to pretrained visual knowledge, while a prior-preservation loss uses images generated by the frozen model to counter class collapse and encourage diverse outputs. Implementations with Imagen and Stable Diffusion support recontextualization, novel viewpoints, artistic renditions, and property modifications. We also provide a public 30-subject dataset and evaluation protocol, using DINO embedding similarity to assess subject identity alongside prompt alignment. Across 3,000 generated images, the Stable Diffusion implementation improves DINO similarity from 0.569 to 0.668 and CLIP text-image similarity from 0.255 to 0.305 compared to Textual Inversion. User comparisons favor DreamBooth for subject fidelity (68% versus 22%) and prompt fidelity (81% versus 12%). An Imagen ablation shows that prior preservation reduces class collapse and increases diversity at a modest cost to subject fidelity. Rare contexts, context-appearance entanglement, overfitting, and hallucinated details remain failure modes.
cases.notes: Centered subject-preserving personalization rather than fine-tuning alone: rare identifiers and class priors enable instance-specific generation. Tables 1-2 support both identity and prompt fidelity against Textual Inversion on Stable Diffusion. Retained the public evaluation resource and DINO metric as co-contributions. Table 3 establishes a diversity/prior-retention tradeoff, not an improvement in every metric. Application examples support capabilities, not universal identity preservation; failure modes delimit them.

cases.abstract: Toolformer trains a language model to select, invoke, and incorporate external tools using supervision derived from its own next-token predictions. Starting from a few demonstrations per text-based API, the model proposes calls in ordinary text; executed calls are retained only when their responses reduce prediction loss relative to omitting the call or its result. Fine-tuning on the augmented corpus teaches tool use without downstream-task demonstrations. We apply this approach to GPT-J with question answering, Wikipedia search, arithmetic, translation, and calendar APIs. In prompted zero-shot evaluations allowing at most one call, Toolformer exceeds GPT-J baselines on factual completion, arithmetic, question answering, and temporal tasks, including a new template-generated DATESET benchmark. On ASDiv, calculator-enabled first-number accuracy reaches 40.4%, versus 14.8% with calls disabled and 14.0% for GPT-3 (175B). Question answering nevertheless remains below GPT-3, and translation improves the tool-trained model without consistently surpassing original GPT-J across languages. With calls disabled, language-modeling perplexity matches content-matched fine-tuning without API annotations. Most tool benefits emerge around 775M parameters in three-tool scaling experiments, with search an exception. Chained and interactive tool use remain unsupported.
cases.notes: Centered the loss-based self-supervision criterion, not the tool list. ASDiv's enabled-versus-disabled comparison tests actual tool access under first-number scoring; GPT-3 comparisons are benchmark-specific, not budget-matched. Retained DATESET as an evaluation co-contribution and preserved weaker question-answering and mixed multilingual findings. Language-modeling preservation is relative to content-matched fine-tuning with calls disabled, not unchanged performance versus original GPT-J. Scaling uses three tools; search is an exception. Single-call evaluation and absent chained/interactive training bound the contribution.
